deck: West Coast gasoline rose again as the U.S. average eased. The widening fuel-cost divide is landing unevenly on households and Western businesses.

signals.headline: Western fuel costs climb as U.S. gasoline eases
signals.body:
The fuel shock is becoming distinctly Western. In the week ending September 28, national regular gasoline slipped 1.3 cents to $4.47 a gallon. West Coast regular rose another 12.4 cents to $5.72. California reached $6.19, up 18.6 cents in a week; San Francisco reached $6.27.

Diesel remained more elevated: $6.41 a gallon in the Rockies, $7.36 on the West Coast and $8.18 in California, against $6.38 nationally. Even within the Rockies, the two fuels moved differently: gasoline eased while diesel rose.

The regional split points toward constraints in refining and finished fuel products alongside the crude-oil shock. It also means the burden is shifting unevenly across the economy. Households face different gasoline costs depending on where they live, while freight, agriculture, construction and other fuel-intensive businesses remain exposed to diesel. A modest decline in the national gasoline average offers little reassurance to a Western operator whose fuel bill is still rising.

signals.headline: Mortgage rates reach 7.28%, delaying the housing thaw
signals.body:
Freddie Mac’s average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.28% on October 1, from 7.03% a week earlier. It was the largest weekly increase in roughly four years and the highest level in nearly three. Mortgage applications were already weakening before this latest setback.

The national move carries particular weight across Western markets where buyers must finance already-high home prices. Higher borrowing costs deepen an affordability constraint that already limits who can buy. The hoped-for 2026 housing thaw is being delayed again.

The pressure also reaches new supply. UCLA Anderson’s September 30 forecast identified elevated mortgage rates as one reason California housing construction remains near roughly 110,000 annual permits, well below estimated need. Expensive financing leaves the state facing both sides of its housing problem: buyers struggle to afford existing homes, while construction remains insufficient to close the gap. A weaker market does not necessarily make an undersupplied region more affordable.

signals.headline: Corn stocks rise 35% while wheat inventories tighten
signals.body:
The Plains agricultural economy faces two different supply signals. USDA’s September 30 Grain Stocks report put U.S. old-crop corn inventories at 2.10 billion bushels, up 35% from a year earlier. Corn held on farms rose 22%; off-farm stocks increased 44%.

Wheat moved in the opposite direction. Inventories totaled 1.85 billion bushels, down 14% from a year earlier, while durum stocks fell 13%. The contrast matters across Nebraska, Kansas, the Dakotas and the broader Plains, where a single description of grain supply would miss the divergence.

For corn producers, heavier inventories bring storage pressure and the prospect of price pressure. Wheat producers face a considerably tighter supply backdrop. Those differences also run through feed and livestock economics: the implications of abundant corn differ from those of scarcer wheat. The inventory figures establish that contrast; they do not, on their own, settle where either market’s prices go next.

source.label: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service · Grain Stocks

signals.headline: A $3 billion-plus shipyard breaks ground in Brownsville
signals.body:
Saronic broke ground September 30 on Port Alpha at the Port of Brownsville, bringing one of South Texas’s largest new industrial investments into construction. The reported plans call for more than $3 billion in private investment, as many as 10,000 direct jobs and approximately 150,000 gross tons of annual shipbuilding capacity at opening.

The employment and capacity figures describe the project’s plans. Its full buildout and hiring still lie ahead, but the announced private investment alone makes this a substantial addition to the region’s industrial base.

Port Alpha fits a broader regional investment pattern increasingly centered on defense, energy, semiconductors, batteries, AI and data infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing. Conventional office-sector expansion is playing a less central role in that picture. For South Texas, shipbuilding is becoming a major part of that capital-investment picture.

source.label: Office of the Governor of Texas

signals.headline: California outgrows the U.S. with unemployment at 5.1%
signals.body:
California continues to generate stronger output growth than employment growth. UCLA Anderson’s September 30 forecast reported first-quarter GDP growth of 3.7% annualized, compared with 2.1% nationally. On a year-over-year basis, California grew 3.3%, against 2.7% for the U.S.

Yet the state’s unemployment rate was 5.1% in August, the highest among U.S. states. It has remained above 5% for 31 months. UCLA describes the situation as an ongoing “employment recession,” even as California captured 82% of U.S. venture-capital investment in the second quarter.

The contrast is central to the West’s technology-led expansion. Strong output and concentrated capital investment, particularly in technology, AI and related industries, are not translating into a traditional broad employment boom. California shows how different the signals can be for investors, businesses and people seeking work. Its growth figures remain strong; the employment record makes clear why output alone is an incomplete measure of how widely that growth is being felt.
